paragraphs: The paper studies how to release an ordered list of the k most frequent elements while protecting the people represented in the data. The challenge is to select useful high-count elements under differential privacy. Its proposed algorithm treats the entire output sequence as one joint choice made by the exponential mechanism.

That joint formulation creates an enormous collection of possible outputs: for a domain containing d elements, there are O(d^k) candidate sequences. The main contribution is a way to sample from this mechanism efficiently despite that output space. The sampling procedure takes O(dk log(k) + d log(d)) time and O(dk) space, making the computational cost much smaller than explicitly considering every sequence.

Experiments report better performance than existing methods providing pure differential privacy. For moderate values of k, the method also improves on methods using approximate differential privacy. These findings show that jointly selecting the sequence can be practically useful, with the efficient sampler making that approach computationally accessible.
icml-2022-a-joint-exponential-mechanism-.tldr: An efficient sampler makes joint differentially private top-k selection practical and delivers reported improvements over existing private methods.

paragraphs: Policy optimization methods can begin from different interpretations of a model or different learning objectives, even though they all seek higher expected return. This paper looks for shared structure in the updates these methods actually perform. The aim is to make their similarities and differences easier to identify within a common mathematical description.

The authors express those updates through a limited selection of gradient forms and scaling functions. This produces a structured, parameterized family of approximate gradient updates that includes both classical and recent methods, including PPO. The parameters describe meaningful choices within the update, providing a way to move beyond the specific combinations used by established algorithms.

Using this family, the paper derives new updates that generalize existing approaches. Experiments in synthetic settings and popular deep reinforcement learning benchmarks show that the additional flexibility can improve convergence speed and final performance. The contribution is therefore both an organizing framework and a route to useful algorithm variants, with benefits demonstrated empirically.
icml-2022-a-parametric-class-of-approxim.tldr: A unified family of approximate policy gradients reveals connections between algorithms and enables updates with demonstrated learning improvements.

paragraphs: Clustering with outliers requires balancing two goals: finding good clusters and limiting how many observations are discarded. This paper adapts familiar sampling-based k-means algorithms to that setting. It improves theoretical guarantees for both sequential algorithms and distributed algorithms, where the computation is spread across multiple participants.

The central guarantee permits (1 + epsilon)z outliers, where z is the true outlier count, while achieving an O(1/epsilon) approximation to the clustering objective. This exposes an explicit tradeoff: demanding an outlier count closer to z weakens the approximation bound. The earlier k-means++ adaptation discussed in the paper instead allowed O(log(k)z) outliers to retain an O(log k) approximation.

A further result gives an O(nk²/z)-time algorithm with constant-factor objective approximation and O(z) outliers, assuming k is much smaller than z and z is much smaller than n. A matching lower bound holds in the oracle model. Under that setting, the runtime result is supported by a corresponding theoretical barrier.
icml-2022-adapting-k-means-algorithms-fo.tldr: Adaptations of classical k-means algorithms offer stronger tradeoffs between clustering quality and the number of discarded outliers.

paragraphs: Primate vision is often treated as a model for robust artificial perception. One associated belief is that reproducing the brain's visual representations should make artificial systems resistant to adversarial image perturbations. This paper examines the biological side of that argument by asking whether those neural representations themselves are resistant to such attacks.

The authors develop a method for directing adversarial visual attacks at primate brain activity. This makes biological neural responses an explicit target of the attack procedure and enables an assessment of their susceptibility. The study reports that the magnitude of this susceptibility is comparable to that of existing artificial neural networks trained for robustness.

The finding challenges the assumption that biological visual representations necessarily provide a more robust target for artificial systems to imitate. Its scope is the measured vulnerability of neural representations to adversarial perturbations. The paper presents this as evidence that the broader belief may be poorly founded, rather than establishing that biological and artificial visual systems are equivalent in every aspect of perception.
icml-2022-adversarially-trained-neural-r.tldr: Attacks targeting primate brain activity reveal susceptibility comparable in magnitude to robustly trained artificial neural networks.

paragraphs: Privacy in machine learning involves different questions about what an attacker can discover. Membership inference asks whether a particular record appeared in training, while reconstruction concerns recovering training data. This paper focuses on reconstruction, motivated by the fact that membership status may itself be harmless to reveal even when the underlying information needs protection.

The authors derive semantic guarantees for differential privacy mechanisms against reconstruction attacks under a formal threat model. Such guarantees connect privacy accounting to the meaning of protection for an attacker pursuing this specific objective. The paper also argues that existing membership-focused guarantees can overestimate an adversary's capabilities, making a reconstruction-focused analysis valuable.

The analysis considers two distinct accounting approaches: Rényi differential privacy and Fisher information leakage. Both are shown to provide strong semantic protection against data reconstruction within the formal setting. The contribution gives a direct theoretical interpretation of protection against recovering training data, with its claims tied to the stated threat model.
icml-2022-bounding-training-data-reconst.tldr: The paper derives formal reconstruction-attack guarantees using Rényi differential privacy and Fisher information leakage.

paragraphs: Different datasets can describe overlapping pieces of a causal system without observing all its variables together. This paper asks how those pieces can constrain counterfactual inference: reasoning about what would have happened under a different intervention. Its starting point is a collection of structural causal models, each covering a different but overlapping set of variables.

The task is to determine which joint causal models are counterfactually consistent with all the smaller models. The authors formalize this problem for categorical variables using a response-function representation. Requiring the pieces to fit together reduces the possible models at both the marginal and joint levels, making compatibility itself a source of information.

This creates a way to challenge causal explanations by bringing additional variables into the analysis. An explanation that is acceptable for one subset may fail to fit the larger collection consistently. The result highlights how expanding the variables considered can restrict causal possibilities, beyond the familiar strategy of collecting more observations of the same variables.
icml-2022-causal-inference-through-the-s.tldr: Combining overlapping causal models constrains counterfactual explanations and creates opportunities to falsify them through additional variables.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples to supplement labeled training data. A common step assigns provisional labels to examples whose predictions exceed a confidence threshold. This paper identifies a problem when classes are imbalanced: using the same fixed threshold across classes contributes to poor performance on classes with fewer examples.

The proposed framework gives different classes adaptive thresholds. It does this by explicitly optimizing how many pseudo-labels each class contributes within the learning objective, jointly determining those quantities while minimizing empirical risk. Threshold selection becomes part of the optimization process, allowing the treatment of unlabeled examples to respond to class differences.

The thresholds have a closed-form solution, making their determination efficient. Experiments across more than twenty imbalance ratios report substantial performance improvements and support the effectiveness of the approach. The contribution is a relatively simple change to the pseudo-label selection mechanism, addressing a specific source of difficulty when semi-supervised learning is applied to uneven class distributions.
icml-2022-class-imbalanced-semi-supervis.tldr: Optimizing class-specific pseudo-label counts yields efficient adaptive confidence thresholds that improve semi-supervised learning under class imbalance.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience across training tasks to support learning on unseen tasks. PAC-Bayesian bounds provide theoretical guarantees for this transfer, but how tight those guarantees can be remains an important question. The paper develops a common framework for analyzing both ordinary single-task learning and meta-learning.

Within that framework, the authors extend the kl-bound and Catoni-bound to standard meta-learning and obtain fast convergence rates. Minimizing the resulting bounds produces two algorithms for classification with deep neural networks. This connects the theoretical analysis to training objectives: the guarantees help define how the meta-learner is optimized.

For regression, choosing a Gibbs optimal posterior for each training task yields a closed-form minimizer of the Catoni-bound and an efficient algorithm. The kl-bound lacks such a closed-form minimizer, but its analysis can extend to tasks whose samples are interdependent. Experiments report competitive performance against recent methods, complementing the contribution of tighter theory and bound-driven algorithm design.
icml-2022-fast-rate-pac-bayesian-general.tldr: A unified PAC-Bayesian framework yields fast-rate meta-learning guarantees and algorithms built by minimizing those bounds.

paragraphs: Many machine learning objectives admit multiple optimal solutions, sometimes infinitely many. Finding a single solution leaves that variety unexplored. This paper studies how to obtain a collection of distinct solutions within the optimum set, so that diversity becomes an explicit goal alongside success on the main optimization problem.

The authors express the task as a bilevel optimization problem: maximize a diversity score while staying within the set of solutions that optimize the main loss. Their population gradient descent framework updates a group of points repeatedly. Those updates seek greater diversity in a way designed not to harm optimization of the main objective.

The method is demonstrated on text-to-image generation, text-to-mesh generation, molecular conformation generation, and neural network ensemble training. Across these applications, the authors show efficient generation of diverse solutions. The contribution offers a shared optimization approach for situations where several good answers are useful, with diversity evaluated inside the main objective's optimum set.
icml-2022-how-to-fill-the-optimum-set-po.tldr: Population gradient descent seeks diverse optimal solutions while preserving optimization of the main loss.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation often assumes that observed data determine the correct correspondence between two domains. This paper asks when that assumption is justified. Even if a correct one-to-one mapping exists, the available observations may leave several mappings plausible. Establishing identifiability means showing that the data distinguish the correct correspondence.

The authors provide several sufficient conditions for identifying linear domain maps. Their analysis shows that weak constraints on third-moment tensors can suffice, and establishes identifiability for common latent-variable models, including topic models. They also develop a computationally tractable method for producing certificates of identifiability, giving a way to substantiate uniqueness in the studied setting.

The certification method motivates a new domain-mapping objective that explicitly represents uncertainty arising when maps are unidentifiable. The paper demonstrates improvements in uncertainty quantification and model performance estimation. Its contribution combines conditions that establish when a mapping can be uniquely determined with an objective that accounts for ambiguity when uniqueness is unavailable.
icml-2022-identifiability-conditions-for.tldr: Sufficient conditions and practical certificates establish identifiability of linear domain maps, while a new objective accounts for mapping ambiguity.

paragraphs: Raw audio contains long sequences because waveforms are sampled at high rates. Modeling them therefore requires an architecture that can handle extended temporal structure without unfavorable computational costs. The paper introduces SaShiMi, a multiscale waveform model built around S4, a model designed for long sequences.

The authors identify instability in S4 during autoregressive generation, where generated samples feed into subsequent predictions. They improve its parameterization using a connection to Hurwitz matrices. SaShiMi achieves reported state-of-the-art unconditional autoregressive waveform generation, and it also improves non-autoregressive generation when used as the backbone of a diffusion model.

Human evaluations favor its piano outputs for musicality and speech outputs for coherence. On one unconditional speech task, its mean opinion score is twice WaveNet's. On a music task, it improves density estimation and both training and inference speed while using three times fewer parameters than WaveNet. These results connect the architecture's long-sequence design to measured improvements in generation quality and computation.
icml-2022-its-raw-audio-generation-with-.tldr: SaShiMi combines multiscale state-space modeling with an improved S4 parameterization to advance raw audio generation quality and efficiency.

paragraphs: Automatically searching for graph neural network architectures becomes difficult on large graphs because evaluating candidate designs is expensive. Existing search methods also encounter consistency collapse. This paper introduces GAUSS to address both the computational burden and the instability involved in estimating and comparing architecture performance.

GAUSS uses a lightweight supernet with graph sampling and a single-path, one-shot design. It jointly considers which architecture and which graph portion to sample. Architecture peer learning on sampled subgraphs and architecture importance sampling help smooth the highly nonconvex objective and stabilize architecture sampling, connecting the search procedure to the data portions used for evaluation.

The authors provide theoretical analyses and experiments on five datasets spanning ten thousand to one hundred million vertices. GAUSS shows substantial improvements over other graph architecture search baselines on every evaluated dataset. The authors also describe it, to their knowledge, as the first such framework to handle graphs with billions of edges within one GPU day.
icml-2022-large-scale-graph-neural-archi.tldr: GAUSS combines an efficient supernet with joint architecture and graph sampling to scale graph architecture search to billions of edges.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from existing data without further environment interaction. Large discrete action spaces create a particular difficulty: many possible actions fall outside the data distribution, making their values difficult to estimate accurately. The paper targets this problem in settings such as recommendation and dialogue, where the number of available actions can be large.

The proposed framework learns action representations through a pseudometric that measures both behavioral relationships and relationships arising from the data distribution. Relative distances between actions are central to the design. The aim is to organize actions in a way that helps reduce the influence of out-of-distribution actions on offline learning.

The authors analyze continuity of expected Q-values and offline policy improvement with the learned representations. Experiments show significant improvements when the framework is applied to two typical offline reinforcement learning methods in large discrete action spaces. The results support using behavior and data coverage together when constructing representations for actions in this setting.
icml-2022-learning-pseudometric-based-ac.tldr: Action representations based on behavioral and data-distribution relationships improve offline reinforcement learning with large discrete action spaces.

paragraphs: Human-provided symbolic descriptions can help reinforcement learning agents organize long tasks, but those descriptions are often incomplete. Earlier approaches commonly assume that symbolic actions can be executed at the lower level and that symbolic state descriptions cover all desirable states. This paper develops an approach that explicitly accommodates incomplete symbolic knowledge.

The authors formalize the relationship between a symbolic model and the underlying Markov decision process, making the model's incompleteness something the framework can characterize. They extract high-level landmarks from the symbolic description to divide the task into subgoals. For each subgoal, the agent learns a collection of diverse low-level policies, which are subsequently combined.

Evaluations across three benchmark domains show that the approach can discover task structure and efficiently guide an agent toward its goal despite incomplete symbolic information. The contribution connects approximate high-level guidance with diversity in learned skills, allowing a task description to provide useful organization without requiring it to specify every detail of successful execution.
icml-2022-leveraging-approximate-symboli.tldr: Incomplete symbolic models guide task decomposition, while diverse learned skills help reinforcement learning agents reach the resulting subgoals.

paragraphs: Many reinforcement learning algorithms are motivated by general policy improvement or trust-region learning. The paper identifies a gap between those theoretical motivations and scalable implementations: practical algorithms use regularization or other choices that violate the original frameworks' assumptions. Describing them as approximations can therefore leave their success insufficiently explained.

Mirror Learning introduces a broader theoretical framework that provides guarantees for a large class of algorithms, including TRPO and PPO. Within it, general policy improvement and trust-region learning appear as highly restrictive special cases. The broader formulation gives theoretical room to algorithmic choices that fall outside those earlier frameworks.

The authors argue that this perspective suggests a more direct connection between successful methods' theoretical properties and their empirical performance. That interpretation is presented as a suggestion, rather than a demonstration that theory explains every practical outcome. The framework also opens a space for developing additional policy optimization algorithms whose designs can be supported by its guarantees.
icml-2022-mirror-learning-a-unifying-fra.tldr: Mirror Learning broadens policy optimization theory to provide guarantees for algorithms including TRPO and PPO.

paragraphs: Inductive logic programming seeks rules that explain facts. This paper introduces Hierarchical Rule Induction, a neuro-symbolic model that combines learning with an explicit structure for constructing interpretable rules. Its starting point is a predefined hierarchy of meta-rules, which serve as templates from which more specific first-order rules can be formed.

The model learns embeddings that match facts and the predicates appearing in the bodies of these templates. The authors design a generic collection of meta-rules and show that it generates a fragment of Horn clauses. Because the model is differentiable, it can be trained through either supervised learning or reinforcement learning.

To encourage interpretable results, training includes controlled noise intended to avoid local optima and a regularization term aimed at interpretability. The authors evaluate the model on logic programming, Visual Genome, and reinforcement learning tasks against relevant traditional and neuro-symbolic methods. The work brings rule construction, gradient-based learning, and an explicit push toward readable rules into one framework.
icml-2022-neuro-symbolic-hierarchical-ru.tldr: Hierarchical Rule Induction learns interpretable logical rules through differentiable matching within a hierarchy of rule templates.

paragraphs: Learning fluid dynamics commonly requires supervision containing particle positions and velocities over time. NeuroFluid tackles a partially observed setting in which the available evidence is a sequence of images of the fluid surface. The goal is to infer the hidden particle transitions and interactions that produce those visible changes.

The approach joins two differentiable components. A particle-driven neural renderer incorporates physical fluid properties into volume rendering, connecting particle descriptions to images. A particle transition model predicts changes in the particle system and is optimized to reduce discrepancies between rendered images and observed images. Training the two components jointly links visual agreement to learning the underlying dynamics.

The authors present this as the first solution for unsupervised learning of particle-based fluid dynamics. Their results show reasonable estimates of underlying fluid physics across different initial shapes, viscosities, and densities. The contribution demonstrates how surface observations can supervise a coupled rendering and dynamics model without requiring the consecutive particle-property supervision used by existing approaches.
icml-2022-neurofluid-fluid-dynamics-grou.tldr: NeuroFluid jointly learns particle dynamics and rendering from fluid-surface images, producing reasonable estimates of hidden physical behavior.

paragraphs: The paper studies a buyer repeatedly offered items with a price and an incomplete description. Each item comes from an unknown distribution, and the buyer must decide whether to purchase it using the masked information. The learning objective is to maximize utility while gradually improving these decisions across T rounds.

Performance is measured against a myopic oracle that knows the item distribution and the seller's masking function. Regret captures the buyer's accumulated shortfall relative to that benchmark. The authors formulate the interaction as an online learning problem and give algorithms with no-regret guarantees under two different sets of conditions.

When the item distribution is known and masking uses SimHash from d-dimensional inputs to length-ell binary outputs, regret scales as the square root of Td ell, up to logarithmic factors. With an arbitrary mask taking n possible values and stochastic prices, the fully agnostic result scales as the square root of Tn. These bounds formalize how learning can reduce average regret despite partial item information.
icml-2022-no-regret-learning-in-partiall.tldr: Online purchasing algorithms achieve conditional no-regret guarantees when buyers see prices and masked item information.

paragraphs: In partial label learning, an example comes with a set of candidate labels whose ambiguity must be resolved during training. Existing approaches commonly favor the candidate with the smallest loss or assign weights representing how likely each candidate is to be correct. This paper investigates another source of information: how a candidate label affects the predictive model.

Inspired by influence functions, the authors develop the PLL-IF framework. The central change in perspective is to consider a label through its influence on the model, bringing the consequences of a candidate choice into the disambiguation process. This supplies a different basis for handling uncertain labels than relying solely on their current loss or likelihood weights.

The framework is implemented with both a support vector machine and a neural network, producing PLL-IF+SVM and PLL-IF+NN. Experiments across various datasets report superior prediction accuracy for the proposed methods. These results support the effectiveness of the influence-based perspective in the evaluated settings and demonstrate its use with two distinct predictive model families.
icml-2022-partial-label-learning-via-lab.tldr: PLL-IF resolves candidate-label ambiguity by considering labels' influence on the predictive model, with reported accuracy improvements.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning a policy from fixed data when the environment is only partially observable, including settings with potentially infinite state and observation spaces. Under an undercompleteness assumption, optimal policies can be characterized through finite-memory Bellman operators. Estimating those operators is difficult when observations are numerous and the dataset provides incomplete coverage.

The proposed algorithm estimates reproducing-kernel Hilbert space embeddings of the operators and uses them to construct confidence regions. It then plans pessimistically within those regions. This makes uncertainty from offline estimation part of the policy selection process, addressing the risk of relying on poorly supported operator estimates.

The authors prove an epsilon-optimal policy guarantee using approximately O(1/epsilon²) episodes, up to logarithmic factors, provided the behavior policy covers the optimal trajectory well. The guarantee therefore retains a specific coverage requirement without demanding uniform coverage. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first provably sample-efficient offline algorithm for partially observable Markov decision processes with that relaxation.
icml-2022-provably-efficient-offline-rei.tldr: Confidence regions and pessimistic planning yield a sample-efficiency guarantee for offline POMDP learning under undercompleteness and optimal-trajectory coverage.

paragraphs: Imbalanced regression occurs when many training examples occupy a small part of the target range. Unlike class labels, regression targets have a natural ordering and meaningful relationships across different values. RankSim uses that structure to guide the features learned by a neural network, especially when the distribution of target values is uneven.

For each example, the method compares two neighbor rankings: one determined by target values and another determined by learned features. Its regularizer encourages those rankings to agree. Examples close in target space should also be close in feature space, and the ranking comparison captures relationships involving both nearby and distant examples.

RankSim can complement reweighting, two-stage training, and distribution smoothing, making it compatible with several existing approaches to imbalance. The paper reports advances in state-of-the-art performance on IMDB-WIKI-DIR, AgeDB-DIR, and STS-B-DIR. These results support the usefulness of shaping feature relationships according to target ordering as an additional signal for learning from imbalanced regression data.
icml-2022-ranksim-ranking-similarity-reg.tldr: RankSim improves imbalanced regression by encouraging learned features to preserve neighbor rankings defined by target values.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents commonly absorb experience into network parameters through gradient updates. Integrating an experience can require substantial computation and many updates, and the model's capacity limits what it retains. This paper adds direct access to stored experience so that an agent's behavior can also depend on information retrieved when needed.

A learned neural retrieval process selects information that may help in the current context. Its dataset can contain the agent's own experiences, expert demonstrations, or other relevant material. At test time, the resulting agent can condition behavior on the dataset beyond its current state or trajectory, giving stored experience an additional route to affect decisions.

The authors integrate retrieval into offline DQN and online R2D2. On offline multitask problems, the augmented DQN avoids task interference and learns faster than baseline DQN. On Atari, augmented R2D2 learns significantly faster and achieves higher scores than baseline R2D2. Ablation studies examine component contributions, supporting the practical value of retrieval in these evaluated settings.
icml-2022-retrieval-augmented-reinforcem.tldr: Learned retrieval gives reinforcement learning agents direct access to past experience and improves learning in evaluated offline and online settings.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks can require computing resources beyond the reach of small research groups. Pooling resources offers a way for several groups to train a shared model on public data. However, this arrangement introduces a reliability problem: one participant can threaten the training run by submitting incorrect updates, either accidentally or deliberately.

Byzantine-tolerant training algorithms address the presence of such participants. Their safeguards often come with communication costs, such as sending redundant information or routing updates through a trusted server. The paper identifies these costs as a major obstacle when the models being trained contain billions of parameters.

The authors propose a decentralized training protocol that combines Byzantine tolerance with an emphasis on communication efficiency. Its contribution targets the tension between protecting a collaborative training run and keeping coordination affordable at large scale. In this setting, security concerns the effect of faulty or malicious training updates, while the broader motivation is making shared computational resources useful for training large models.
icml-2022-secure-distributed-training-at.tldr: A decentralized Byzantine-tolerant training protocol emphasizes communication efficiency for collaborative large-model training.

paragraphs: Sparse neural networks are attractive because they reduce the number of parameters that must be trained and stored and can improve learning efficiency. Their use has grown in computer vision, while deep reinforcement learning has received comparatively little attention. This paper systematically examines how existing sparse training methods behave in that setting.

The investigation applies multiple sparse training techniques across different reinforcement learning agents and environments. Its central empirical result is that sparse networks outperform dense networks with the same parameter count. Holding parameter count fixed matters for interpreting the comparison: the reported advantage concerns how the available parameters are organized within the evaluated networks.

The authors also analyze how individual components of deep reinforcement learning are affected by sparsity. They use those analyses to identify promising directions for improving sparse training methods and expanding their use. The study supplies evidence that a finding previously observed in computer vision also appears in reinforcement learning, while examining the consequences within the learning system.
icml-2022-the-state-of-sparse-training-i.tldr: A systematic study finds sparse networks outperform dense networks at equal parameter counts in evaluated deep reinforcement learning settings.

paragraphs: Inferring how cells change type is difficult when individual cells cannot be followed over time. Cells observed at the same real-world time may also occupy different stages of a transition, and one starting cell type can branch toward several outcomes. The paper treats these difficulties as learning a dynamical system from observations with unknown timing.

The proposed model combines a deep generative approach with a simple family of ordinary differential equations informed by gene-expression biochemistry. Those equations constrain the model's likelihood. The resulting system jointly infers each cell's latent time and state, while predicting its future gene expression. Its dynamics form a mixture of ODEs whose parameters vary continuously across the latent space of cell states.

The authors report substantial improvements over previous approaches in data fit, latent-time inference, and future-state estimation. These findings support combining biochemical structure with flexible latent representations to infer cellular dynamics. The approach addresses both uncertainty about a cell's position in a transition and variation among possible developmental paths.
icml-2022-variational-mixtures-of-odes-f.tldr: A biochemically informed mixture of ODEs infers cellular transition timing and state while improving predictions of future gene expression.
